results.result: The manuscript provides background on enhancers and their modes of interaction based on prior literature. Previous studies have shown that enhancers can combine additively, supra-additively (synergistically), or sub-additively (redundantly), but these studies tested only small numbers of enhancers in limited genomic loci.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work and accurately represent the state of knowledge in the field. These claims establish the scientific context and motivation for the current study.

results.result: The authors developed a three-way combinatorial MPRA to test approximately 69,000 enhancer-enhancer-promoter (EEP) combinations using 8 promoters, 59 enhancers, and 20 control sequences in mouse embryonic stem cells. After quality filtering, activities were determined for 110,180 (55%) combinations including 2,584 control-control, 38,390 enhancer-control, and 69,206 enhancer-enhancer combinations.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C14-C15, C19-C25, C95-C96 describe the experimental design and scale with specific quantitative details. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate references to figures and supplementary materials, and the scale represents a substantial advance over prior work.

results.result: Seven developmental promoters (Klf2, Sox2, Nanog, Otx2, Lefty1, Fgf5, Tbx3) involved in pluripotency regulation and one housekeeping promoter (Ap1m1) were selected. Each promoter included approximately -350 to +50 bp around the transcription start site.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 describe the promoter selection with appropriate citations justifying the choices. The rationale for the promoter region size is supported by prior work (Martinez-Ara et al., 2022; van Arensbergen et al., 2017).

results.result: Developmental promoter libraries showed high replicate correlations (Pearson's R=0.82-0.96), while the housekeeping promoter library showed lower correlations (Pearson's R=0.74-0.78), likely due to smaller dynamic range.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 report replicate reproducibility with specific correlation values and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The interpretation of lower correlation for the housekeeping promoter is reasonable given the stated smaller dynamic range.

results.result: Single enhancers showed little position and orientation dependence. The majority of selected sequences acted as enhancers with significant activation of at least one promoter (FDR<0.01), though boost indices varied up to ~5 log2 units. Enhancers exhibited significant promoter selectivity, with particularly smaller boost indices for the housekeeping promoter.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 describe single enhancer characterization with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR<0.01) and references to figures. The promoter selectivity finding is confirmed by statistical analysis consistent with prior work (Martinez-Ara et al., 2022).

results.result: Enhancer-enhancer combinations were generally more active than enhancer-control combinations and tended to induce stronger activation than single enhancers, although some saturation occurred with the strongest enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 report quantitative comparisons with references to Figure 3. The observation of saturation at high enhancer activities is appropriately qualified as appearing to occur rather than being definitively established.

results.result: For most promoters, an additive model fit the measured data better than a multiplicative model. The multiplicative model tended to overestimate activities at higher ranges for most promoters, except for the Ap1m1 promoter where both models were nearly indistinguishable.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 describe model comparisons with references to figures. The conclusion favoring the additive model is supported by systematic comparison across promoters, though the authors appropriately note the exception for Ap1m1.

results.result: 74.5% of measured enhancer-enhancer activities lie within one standard deviation and 94% within two standard deviations of additive model predictions. Most enhancers combine near-additively, with sub-additive and supra-additive effects being generally rare or weak.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 provide quantitative support for near-additive behavior using an error model. The statistical analysis with specific percentages and standard deviation thresholds appropriately supports the conclusion of predominant near-additivity.

results.result: Supra-additivity frequency varied across promoters, with Sox2, Lefty1, Tbx3, and Fgf5 showing relatively high proportions and Ap1m1 showing the lowest. Supra-additivity proportion correlated inversely with promoter baseline expression, with lowly active promoters allowing more supra-additive interactions (though still <40% of pairs). Sub-additive effects were similar across promoters, suggesting no strong saturation effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 describe promoter-dependent supra-additivity with statistical correlations and appropriate quantitative thresholds. The inference about lack of saturation (C50) is reasonably drawn from the observation about sub-additive effects being similar across promoters.

results.result: 32.7% (19/58) of tested enhancers showed consistent supra-additivity in at least one promoter context, while only 10.3% (6/58) showed consistent supra-additivity in two or more promoter contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 provide specific quantitative data on enhancer supra-additivity across promoter contexts with clear thresholds (>0.5 log2 observed/expected) and reference to Figure 4C.

results.result: Enhancer-enhancer combinations from the same genomic locus showed no higher observed/expected ratio than combinations from different loci, indicating no preferential synergy among enhancers from the same locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 report a comparison of within-locus versus between-locus enhancer pairs with reference to Figure 4E. The conclusion of no preferential locus-specific synergy is appropriately drawn from the data showing slightly lower ratios for same-locus pairs.

results.result: All seven developmental promoters showed strong pairwise correlations of boost indices (Pearson's R=0.79-0.98) and correlated strongly with the average pattern (R=0.93-0.99). The housekeeping promoter correlated much less with developmental promoters (R=0.19-0.60) and with the average pattern (R=0.42).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 report correlation analyses with specific values and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The distinction between developmental and housekeeping promoters is clearly supported by the quantitative differences in correlation coefficients.

results.result: Developmental promoters differ in the scaling (steepness) of their responses to enhancer-enhancer pairs despite highly similar response patterns. Slopes relative to averaged promoters ranged fivefold (1.54 to 0.32) and negatively correlated with promoter baseline activity. Promoters with low intrinsic activity respond more steeply to changes in combined enhancer activity. This differential response also occurs with single enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 describe non-linear promoter scaling with quantitative slope analysis and correlation with baseline activity (Figure 5B). The extension to single enhancers (C63) is supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2. This represents a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: This study is much larger scale than previous efforts and found that while a broad spectrum of functional interactions exists, near-additive effects predominate. Supra-additive interactions occur at lower frequency and depend on specific enhancer and promoter context.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 summarize the main findings in context of prior work with appropriate citations. The scale comparison and conclusions about predominant additivity are well-supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Promoters substantially impact supra-additivity of enhancer-enhancer interactions and can be seen as 'interpreters' of enhancer combinations. Different promoters show different degrees of responsiveness, with stronger promoters being boosted less than weaker promoters. Promoter responses follow roughly a power-law function with promoter-dependent exponents, likely below 1 based on observed saturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 synthesize key findings about promoter function with appropriate references to figures. The power-law interpretation and inference about exponents <1 (C72) are reasonably drawn from the log-log scale plots and saturation observations.

results.result: The findings resemble an earlier study (Hong and Cohen, 2022) showing that promoter activities are non-linearly scaled by genomic environment, with steepness negatively correlated with promoter strength.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 appropriately contextualizes the current findings with prior work through citation. This comparison strengthens the interpretation of the results.

results.result: The MPRA reporters were not integrated into the genome, ensuring all combinations were tested under similar conditions without chromatin context confounding. Other studies indicate transiently transfected reporters behave quite similarly to integrated reporters.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 acknowledge a methodological consideration with appropriate citations to prior work (Inoue and Ahituv, 2015; Klein et al., 2020; Maricque et al., 2018) supporting the validity of the episomal approach.

results.result: Results may be biased by the selection of enhancers and promoters focused on pluripotency genes in mouse ESCs, though the three-way MPRA protocol should be generally applicable to any enhancer and promoter set.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 appropriately acknowledge potential limitations while noting the generalizability of the method. This represents appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: In the MPRA, enhancer and promoter elements are in fixed positions close together, not recapitulating genomic positioning. Genomic distance and chromatin contexts could act as thresholds or create non-linear relationships, as shown in prior studies of distance-dependent activation and spacing-dependent synergy.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 acknowledge experimental limitations with appropriate citations to relevant prior work (Zuin et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2022). This represents appropriate discussion of caveats.

results.result: Comparisons with native genomic contexts show mixed results. The current study did not observe synergies reported in the Sox2 locus control region (Brosh et al., 2023), though data are not directly comparable. Results for Fgf5 locus in mESCs align with prior work showing no synergy in this cell type. The default mode of enhancer interplay may be additive, with chromatin context, spacing, and cellular state enabling synergy in some loci.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 appropriately compare findings with prior genomic studies, noting both consistencies and discrepancies with appropriate caveats. The speculation about default additivity (C87) is reasonable given the data but appropriately qualified as 'possibly'.

results.result: Two intermingled factors account for promoter differences: distinct promoter classes show different specificities (illustrated by housekeeping vs. developmental promoters), and promoters scale enhancer pair input differently. The compatibility differences observed in prior work likely reflect both specificity and responsiveness differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 synthesize current and prior findings (Martinez-Ara et al., 2022) to provide a more nuanced interpretation of enhancer-promoter compatibility. The inference is well-supported by the data showing both class-specific and scaling differences.

results.result: The findings have implications for understanding enhancer relevance across loci and promoter sensitivity to activating signals. Quantifying promoter responsiveness genome-wide could reveal which genes are more sensitive to environmental cues or non-coding mutations, particularly relevant for developmentally regulated transcription factors sensitive to dosage changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 discuss implications and future directions appropriately based on the findings. The speculation about future work (C93) is reasonable, and the relevance to developmental genes (C94) is supported by citation to Naqvi et al., 2023.

results.result: DNase hypersensitive sites have been shown to retain enhancer activity individually, supporting the approach of testing smaller elements within enhancer clusters.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 justifies the experimental design choice with appropriate citations to multiple prior studies (Barakat et al., 2018; Agrawal et al., 2021; Bergman et al., 2022; Martinez-Ara et al., 2022).

results.result: The study tested ~69,000 enhancer-enhancer-promoter (EEP) combinations and found that enhancer pairs predominantly combine near-additively. An additive model fit the data better than a multiplicative model for most promoters, with 74.5% of measured EE activities within one standard deviation and 94% within two standard deviations of additive predictions. Sub-additive and supra-additive effects were found to be generally rare or weak.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The editor states the study 'provides solid evidence that enhancers generally combine additively,' and Reviewer 1 notes 'the data in this study do generally support these claims' regarding near-additive combination. Reviewer 2 states 'Both of these findings are interesting and are well supported by the data,' referring to the additive combination as one of two main findings.

results.result: Promoter choice affects enhancer-enhancer interplay, with promoters integrating enhancer effects in a non-linear manner. Weak promoters (Sox2, Lefty1, Tbx3, Fgf5) showed relatively higher proportions of supra-additive EE interactions, while the housekeeping Ap1m1 promoter exhibited the lowest frequency. The proportion of supra-additivity correlated inversely with promoter baseline expression, though supra-additive interactions remained a minority (<40% of EE pairs).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding. The editor notes 'promoters, particularly weaker ones, can exhibit supra-additivity when integrating enhancer effects.' Reviewer 1 calls this 'an interesting result' and notes it 'aligns with the model previously proposed in Hong et al.' Reviewer 2 states 'Both of these findings are interesting and are well supported by the data,' identifying this as one of two main findings.

results.result: Developmental promoters showed strong pairwise correlations in their boost indices (R=0.79-0.98) and correlated strongly with average patterns (R=0.93-0.99), while the housekeeping Ap1m1 promoter correlated much less (R=0.19-0.60 with developmental promoters, R=0.42 with average). Promoters differed in the scaling/steepness of their responses to EE pairs (slopes ranging ~fivefold from 1.54 to 0.32), with relative slopes negatively correlating with baseline promoter activity. Promoters with low intrinsic activity responded more steeply to changes in combined EE activity than those with high intrinsic activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding without critique. Reviewer 1 notes the 'nonlinear promoter response to enhancers aligns with the model previously proposed in Hong et al.' and observes that 'the steepness of the scaling is negatively correlated with promoter strength' (similar to Figure 5b trend). Reviewer 2 finds 'the near equivalence of Fig. 5b and Fig. S7b is intriguing,' indicating acceptance of the promoter scaling relationship.

results.result: The majority of tested enhancers exhibited significant preference for certain promoters, with variability of enhancer effects across promoters generally larger than expected from experimental noise. This indicates that single enhancers show significant promoter selectivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as confirmatory of previous work. Reviewer 1 notes the paper 'makes a good contribution to the ongoing discussions about the selectivity of gene regulatory elements' and that it 'adds another layer' to previous findings. Reviewer 2 provides methodological clarification about selectivity definition but does not challenge the finding itself, stating the study 'provides the ability to investigate the notion of selectivity.'

results.result: Out of 58 tested enhancers, 32.7% showed consistent supra-additivity in at least one promoter context, and only 10.3% in two or more contexts. EE combinations from the same genomic locus showed no higher observed/expected ratio than combinations from different loci, indicating no preferential synergy among enhancers from the same locus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these specific quantitative findings. Reviewer 1 requested additional analysis about 'enhancers in E-E-P combinations that exhibit supra-additivity' and whether 'certain enhancers...are more likely to show supra-additivity,' which the authors addressed in revision. The revised manuscript 'satisfactorily addresses the points' raised, indicating acceptance of the findings.

results.result: Developmental promoter libraries showed high replicate correlations (R=0.82-0.96), while the housekeeping promoter showed lower correlations (R=0.74-0.78). There was little position and orientation dependence of enhancer effects. The majority of selected sequences acted as enhancers with all showing significant activation of at least one promoter (FDR<0.01), though boost indices were particularly smaller for the Ap1m1 housekeeping promoter.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these quality control and validation findings. Reviewer 2 notes 'Overall this is a nice experimental design and a great dataset' with 'no major concerns,' implicitly accepting the technical quality metrics. The lack of reviewer critique of these methodological details indicates acceptance.

results.result: EE combinations were generally more active than EC combinations and tended to induce stronger activation than single enhancers, though some saturation occurred with the strongest enhancers. The proportion of sub-additive effects was similar across promoters, suggesting no strong saturation effect explaining the decrease in supra-additive interactions as promoter activity increases.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these observations as part of the overall finding of near-additivity. Reviewer 1 notes the data 'generally support these claims' about EE combination patterns. Reviewer 2 states the findings are 'well supported by the data.' The saturation observation is presented as a nuance within the broader additive model, which reviewers affirm.

results.result: Differential responses of promoters (non-linear scaling) can also be observed with single enhancer elements, not just EE pairs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically requested analysis of single enhancers to examine 'if the ability of an enhancer to boost a promoter is inversely correlated to that promoter's intrinsic strength,' and noted in the revised version that 'with the addition of the new graphs there is enough data for readers to decide' about this relationship, indicating the finding is adequately supported.

results.result: The MPRA reporters were not integrated into the genome but tested episomally, ensuring all EEP combinations were tested under similar conditions without confounding chromatin context effects. The enhancer and promoter elements were placed in fixed positions close to one another, not recapitulating their genomic positioning. Previous studies indicate transiently transfected reporters behave quite similarly to integrated reporters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these methodological features without challenging their validity. Reviewer 2 notes 'The authors note many limitations, including the selection of the elements and the size and spacing of the tested elements' and states 'we do not know which mechanisms produce the non-additivity...and which experimental designs would preserve such mechanisms,' indicating acceptance of the experimental design limitations as acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: Previous studies reported synergies in the Sox2 locus control region and Fgf5 locus in native genomic contexts, which the current study did not observe. However, data are not directly comparable due to differences in element sizes and cellular contexts (mESCs vs. differentiated cells). The authors speculate that the default mode of EE interplay may be additive, while chromatin context, element spacing, and cellular state may enable synergy in some loci.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly raises this discrepancy: 'Some of the enhancer-enhancer-promoter triples they test were also investigated by a different experimental design in Brosh et al 2023. Brosh et al observed non-additivity between these elements while this study did not.' The reviewer notes 'Ultimately we do not know which mechanisms produce the non-additivity that has been observed in native loci and which experimental designs would preserve such mechanisms,' indicating uncertainty about how to reconcile the findings.

results.result: The results may be biased by the selection of enhancers and promoters focused on pluripotency genes in mESCs. Genomic distance and chromatin contexts could act as thresholds or turn additive interactions into non-linear relationships, as suggested by reports that distant enhancer pairs are more often synergistic than closely spaced ones.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these limitations without fully resolving them. Reviewer 2 states 'The authors note many limitations, including the selection of the elements and the size and spacing of the tested elements' and notes uncertainty about 'which experimental designs would preserve such mechanisms' of non-additivity. The authors acknowledge they 'cannot rule out' selection bias, indicating this remains an open question.

results.result: Two intermingled factors account for differences between promoters: distinct promoter classes show different specificities (illustrated by poor correlations between Ap1m1 and developmental promoters), and promoters scale enhancer input differently. The compatibility differences from previous studies likely represent a mix of specificity-based and responsiveness-based (intrinsic strength) differences.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation as connecting current and previous findings. Reviewer 1 requested additional analysis to clarify 'how single enhancers can show selectivity for promoters while the effect of adding a second enhancer to an existing E-P has little selectivity,' and noted the revised manuscript 'satisfactorily addresses the points' raised, indicating acceptance of the two-factor explanation.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate claims about additive enhancer combination (C37-C40) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the additive model is favored with exception for Ap1m1. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding, with all reviewers stating the data support near-additive combination. Strong agreement.

Both evaluate claims about near-additive behavior with error model (C41-C44) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative statistical support. Peer reviewers affirm the data support near-additive claims. Strong agreement on this finding.

Both evaluate promoter-dependent supra-additivity (C45-C48) and find it SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes statistical correlations and quantitative thresholds. Peer reviewers call this 'interesting and well supported,' identifying it as one of two main findings. Strong agreement.

Both evaluate correlation analyses distinguishing developmental and housekeeping promoters (C55-C58) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes quantitative differences in correlation coefficients. Peer reviewers affirm the finding without critique. Strong agreement.

Both evaluate non-linear promoter scaling (C59-C62) and find it SUPPORTED. OpenEval identifies this as a key mechanistic finding with quantitative slope analysis. Peer reviewers note alignment with Hong et al. model and accept the negative correlation between scaling steepness and promoter strength. Strong agreement.

Both address single enhancer analysis (C63). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED by Figure 5 supplement 2. Peer reviewer specifically requested this analysis and found adequate data for readers to evaluate the relationship between enhancer boost and promoter strength. Agreement after revision.

Both evaluate power-law interpretation and promoter function (C70-C72). OpenEval finds the inference about exponents <1 reasonably drawn from data. Peer reviewers accept the promoter scaling relationship, with Reviewer 2 finding the equivalence of related figures 'intriguing.' Agreement on interpretation.

Both evaluate promoter selectivity findings (C32-C33) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes statistical confirmation consistent with prior work. Peer reviewers accept this as confirmatory, noting it 'adds another layer' to previous findings. Strong agreement.

Both evaluate replicate reproducibility (C26-C27). OpenEval finds correlation values and interpretation SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these quality control metrics as part of 'nice experimental design and great dataset' with no major concerns. Agreement.

Both evaluate single enhancer characterization (C28-C31). OpenEval finds statistical thresholds and analysis SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept technical quality without questioning these methodological details. Agreement on validation findings.

Both evaluate quantitative data on enhancer supra-additivity across promoters (C51-C52) and find it SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes specific thresholds and figure references. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings and note revised manuscript 'satisfactorily addresses' related questions. Agreement.

Both evaluate within-locus versus between-locus enhancer comparison (C53-C54) and find it SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes no preferential locus-specific synergy. Peer reviewers accept these findings after authors addressed revision requests about supra-additivity patterns. Agreement.

Both evaluate saturation observations (C34-C36, C49-C50). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED with appropriate qualification. Peer reviewers accept these as nuances within the broader additive model they affirm. Agreement on observations as part of near-additivity finding.

Both evaluate episomal approach methodology (C74-C76, C79). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers acknowledge these methodological features and limitations without challenging validity, noting authors appropriately note limitations. Agreement on methodological validity.

Both address generalizability and potential limitations (C77). OpenEval finds appropriate scientific caution SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note UNCERTAIN regarding which experimental designs preserve non-additivity mechanisms, acknowledging authors 'cannot rule out' certain limitations. Partial agreement with more uncertainty from peer reviewers.

Both evaluate experimental limitations (C80, C82). OpenEval finds acknowledgment SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAIN about how limitations affect interpretation, noting uncertainty about which mechanisms are preserved. OpenEval more accepting, peer reviewers more cautious.

Both evaluate comparison with prior genomic studies (C83-C87). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED with appropriate caveats and qualified speculation. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAIN, explicitly raising discrepancy with Brosh et al. 2023 and noting uncertainty about reconciling findings. Significant disagreement: OpenEval accepts with caveats, peer reviewers uncertain about validity.

Both evaluate two-factor explanation of enhancer-promoter compatibility (C89-C90) and find it SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes synthesis of current and prior findings. Peer reviewers accept this interpretation after authors addressed revision requests about reconciling selectivity findings. Agreement after clarification.

OpenEval evaluates background/context claims (C1-C9) establishing scientific motivation and finds them SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation of these introductory claims.

OpenEval evaluates promoter selection rationale (C16-C18) and finds it SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation of these methodological justification claims.
